title: CRAFT: Constrained Route planning with Adaptive Framework and Template-based code generation
summary: Everyday routing requests are rarely a point-to-point shortest path. A driver may need to visit stops, sometimes in a fixed order, under time budgets or distance limits, and perhaps recharge their EV car along the way. Each combination is a distinct routing problem that classically requires its own algorithm, so no fixed solver covers the space of queries users may ask. This paper presents CRAFT, which takes a constrained routing query as free text and returns a route that satisfies the user's requirements on a real road network. An LLM parses the query and generates four search functions, which a generic graph-search engine executes on the road network. We formalize the underlying problem as State-Expanded RCSP (SE-RCSP), which extends resource-constrained shortest paths (RCSP) with non-additive state such as node-dependent resets and discrete progress tracking. We evaluate CRAFT on 2,600 natural-language queries over California road networks against two baselines, analyzing correctness, constraint violations, long-distance scalability, and semantic POI filtering.

title: The American Medical Directory Panel: Comparing AI-Assisted and LLM Transcription with Manual Data Entry at Scale
summary: How closely does machine transcription agree with manual double-entry data? We digitize the 1912 and 1921 editions of the American Medical Directory, a national register of US physicians with roughly 140,000 and 150,000 entries in the two volumes, and compare five machine-extraction workflows with a full-count double-entered manual transcription. Like many historical directories, the AMD is semi-structured rather than tabular, so errors arise from misreading the layout as well as the text. A script that parses commercial OCR text using rules written by coding agents recovers about 97 percent of manually transcribed records with similar precision, more than a multimodal language model workflow (gemini-2.0.flash) that reads the page images and the OCR text. When the two methods fail, they fail on partly overlapping sets of records, so reconciling their outputs raises both recall and precision to about 98 percent. An open-weight LLM pipeline run on a local GPU server falls between the parser and the multimodal workflow in recall, and replacing the commercial OCR model with an open-source alternative lowers its recall by only about 2 percentage points. As the manual transcription's own error rate is unknown, these rates measure agreement rather than accuracy. Direct processing charges for the commercial OCR and multimodal workflow were about 0.03 euro per page, compared with 14.70 euro per page for manual transcription.

title: Standardized Tolerance for Adaptive Reuse and Repair: A Method for HNSW Migration Under Embedding Model Change Scenarios
summary: When an embedding model changes, the same collection is re-encoded, and its vector index must be adapted to the new embedding space. Because the source and target vectors represent the same objects, suitable connections in the source index can be reused. We propose STARR (Standardized Tolerance for Adaptive Reuse and Repair) to migrate HNSW indexes after an embedding model change. STARR compares standardized edge lengths over the same source neighbor lists in both embedding spaces and uses the correlation between their distance profiles to set the allowable increase in standardized edge length. It reconnects affected vertices by searching the partially migrated graph and shares the resulting candidates with their neighbors. We bound edge rejection under local distance distortion, characterize migration work, and prove that a final repair pass makes every vertex reachable from the entry point at the base layer while respecting degree limits. Single-threaded experiments on MS MARCO, Wikipedia, and CC3M, each with one million objects, show that STARR achieves 5.25--44.54$\times$ construction speedups over Fresh and migrates faster than both DGM variants on all 15 selected transitions. Recall@10 remains within one percentage point of Fresh in 10 cases, and query throughput exceeds DGM-Local in 14 cases. Parameter sweeps on three transitions further demonstrate favorable migration-time--recall tradeoffs beyond the default settings. Across all 240 directed transitions among 16 MS MARCO models, STARR achieves a median construction speedup of 16.71$\times$ with a median recall loss of 1.0 percentage point.

title: GenSPARQL: A Generative Extension of SPARQL for Incomplete Knowledge Graphs
comment: 4 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Demo paper submitted to The Web Conference 2027 (WWW 2027). Code: https://github.com/0sidewalkenforcer0/GenSPARQL
summary: Knowledge graphs on the Web are incomplete, and SPARQL answers a query only from the stored triples. Large language models (LLMs) can predict missing facts, but an LLM returns names instead of IRIs and requires one call per binding of a query variable. We present GenSPARQL, a generative extension of SPARQL 1.1 with an operator GENOP that binds values generated by an LLM to query variables during query evaluation. A similarity join maps generated names to entities of the graph, and the query planner invokes the LLM only for the bindings selected by the other graph patterns and filters. In a web workbench, attendees query two graphs built from Wikidata and inspect generated values, mapped entities and LLM calls. In our evaluation with three open-weight LLMs, the embedding similarity maps 83% of the entities named by the LLMs and yields only one incorrect match.

title: Bridging the Discovery Gap in Solid Dataspaces with a Semantic Data Catalog
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 2nd Solid Symposium Poster Session, co-located with the 3rd Solid Symposium, April 24-25, 2025, Leiden, Netherlands
summary: Dataspaces are an emerging concept to enable secure and controlled data sharing between multiple stakeholders. However, most existing dataspace architectures, such as those based on the concepts of IDSA (International Data Spaces Association) and Gaia-X, are heavily concept-driven and require significant effort to implement, making it difficult to quickly build a functional dataspace. Solid (Social Linked Data) offers a compelling alternative by providing a lighter and more practical approach. However, for Solid to function as a true dataspace, like traditional dataspaces, it must be built in a decentralized manner, i.e., the dataspace must consist of more than a single Solid server. However, this decentralization introduces a key challenge: Data Discovery. Unlike traditional dataspace architectures, which often include predefined components such as data catalogs to facilitate data discovery and access, Solid does not inherently provide such mechanisms. As a result, managing and locating relevant data across multiple Solid servers and pods becomes a significant barrier to usability. To address this gap, we present a FAIR-compliant data catalog for Solid. Our catalog follows the FAIR principles (Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reusability) by integrating semantic models that describe all available data sources within the Solid ecosystem. This approach enables enhanced data discovery, improves accessibility through standardized metadata, enhances interoperability between different data sources, and promotes data reuse across applications. By bridging this critical gap, our catalog improves the usability of Solid-based dataspaces, making them a viable option for decentralized and open data ecosystems, such as smart city applications.

title: When Queries Crowd: Diagnosing and Improving Spread-Out Regularization for Text Embeddings
summary: Text embedding models are central to information retrieval and deep research tasks, and their behaviors are strongly shaped by the training objective. While recent systems have largely converged on InfoNCE-style loss functions, there have been continued attempts to design additional loss functions beyond this core objective. One such component is spread-out loss, a batch-level penalty on high pairwise similarity that encourages embeddings to occupy the representation space more evenly. However, in existing systems, this design is usually combined with many other design choices and has not been sufficiently ablated. To isolate its effect, we use spread-out loss as a controlled lens for studying geometric regularization in text embedding training. Across 13 retrieval benchmarks, spread-out improves fine-tuned retrievers over contrastive baselines across architectures and model sizes. We then diagnose where these gains arise and find that they concentrate on short queries, where spread-out reduces query-side directional crowding. Based on this diagnosis, we propose QUARTO, a Query-length Adaptive spread-out loss that uses batch composition to scale the full regularizer more strongly for short-query-dominated batches and less strongly for longer-query-dominated batches. QUARTO further improves retrieval performance over fixed-weight spread-out. Overall, our findings point to the potential of embedding-space regularization and suggest that text-embedding training should explore a broader design space of objectives beyond InfoNCE-style contrastive learning. title: OPTIMIZATION AND IMPLEMENTATION TECHNIQUES FOR HIGH-PERFORMANCE DATABASE PROCEDURES IN THE ORACLE PL/SQL ENVIRONMENT
summary: In modern information systems, databases play a critical role in storing, processing, and managing large volumes of data. As the amount of data and the complexity of database operations increase, ensuring high performance and efficient resource utilization becomes increasingly important. Oracle Database is one of the widely used relational database management systems, offering powerful features for developing and managing database applications. PL/SQL (Procedural Language/Structured Query Language) is Oracle's procedural extension of SQL that enables developers to create stored procedures, functions, packages, and triggers. These program units allow complex business logic to be implemented directly within the database environment, reducing unnecessary communication between applications and database servers. However, poorly designed PL/SQL procedures may lead to slow execution, excessive CPU and memory consumption, and increased database workload. Therefore, optimizing PL/SQL code is essential for improving overall database performance.

title: Memory-Efficient Query Processing for Main-Memory Databases
summary: Abstract (EN) Memory consumption in database systems is a critical issue. While most techniques to reduce memory consumption focus on minimizing table data impact, mitigating the impact of memory consumption imposed by query processing tends to get overlooked. Common techniques, however, exist, and encompass traditional techniques like hash table and probe side partitioning when executing joins, employing data structures with minimal memory footprint during query processing, and compressing intermediate results. The dynamics within allocation of memory consumers on the other hand are not well studied. In modern query processors, we can leverage the dynamics of pipeline execution to optimize memory consumption. In-memory database systems like SAP HANA use pipelining query execution engines to execute queries. For executing pipelines, state-of-the-art engines utilize fine-grained parallelism to fully utilize all available hardware threads. Due to this, only one pipeline should be executed at any time, which necessitates ordering of execution. A direct result of the execution of pipelines are intermediate results. Those intermediate results are contained in so-called pipeline breakers. Pipeline breakers dominate memory consumption in query processing. A pipeline breaker only materializes when a pipeline is executed, hence only consumes memory from this point until deallocation. The intermediate result within pipeline breaker is deallocated once the intermediate result has been consumed. We found that we can lower the memory consumption by optimizing Pipeline Execution Orders (PEOs), which is the execution order of executable pipelines in query engines. This opportunity is enabled by effectively changing the time when pipeline breakers materialize through this ordering. Within this doctoral thesis, I explore the optimization of memory consumption by enumerating PEOs and assigning them with memory consumption estimates. I show that we can effectively lower the memory consumption by up to 11.1% in a pipelining engine prototype with strong confidence. I established mathematical methods to precisely calculate the enumeration overhead of our approach. I further implemented our approach in an industrial database system prototype with my component called PEOopt, which can contribute memory consumption reduction up to 36%.

title: A Comparative Performance Evaluation of SQL and NoSQL Databases Under Different Indexing and Cache Conditions
summary: This study presents a comparative benchmark of MySQL 8.0. 46 and MongoDB 8.0. 32 using bulk-write, point-lookup, and filtered-aggregation workloads. Experiments were conducted on a single Ubuntu-based computer using synthetic transaction datasets containing 10K, 100K, and 1M records. Performance was measured under unindexed, indexed, and warm-cache conditions, with five measured iterations per configuration. MongoDB recorded lower bulk-write latency at all dataset sizes. Single-field indexing substantially reduced point-lookup latency in both database systems, with reductions exceeding 99% at one million records. Aggregation results varied according to dataset size and configuration. At one million records, MySQL's indexed aggregation latency was higher than its unindexed latency; an independent remeasurement reproduced this result under the tested conditions. These findings demonstrate that database performance depends on workload, dataset size, indexing, and execution state. The study does not establish a universal advantage for either database model. Instead, it provides a controlled, single-host comparison and identifies directions for further investigation, including composite indexes, concurrent workloads, and distributed deployments.

title: Optimal multi-objective configuration of a hybrid walker-star/delta navigation satellite constellation in LEO via MOPSO and reinforcement learning
summary: Optimal design of satellite constellations in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) for global navigation and positioning applications is of significant importance. This study presents a design framework for LEO satellite constellations based on hybrid Walker-Star/Delta geometric configurations, with the objective of simultaneously minimizing Geometric Dilution of Precision (GDOP) and deployment costs. A multi-objective optimization approach is employed by integrating Multi-Objective Particle Swarm Optimization (MOPSO) with Reinforcement Learning (RL) to adaptively tune key optimization parameters and the resulting RL-MOPSO algorithm is validated against conventional MOPSO and NSGA-II on standard benchmark problems. Satellite manufacturing and launch costs are estimated using a combined SSCM/USCM8 cost model and the design tool is further validated against the operational GLONASS constellation. The proposed hybrid configuration is evaluated against conventional Walker-Delta and Walker-Star configurations across multiple orbital altitudes. Results show that the optimized hybrid configuration achieves a notable improvement in mean GDOP compared with both Walker-Delta and Walker-Star configurations, while maintaining a comparable number of satellites and avoiding any significant increase in deployment cost. These findings demonstrate that the proposed RL-MOPSO based hybrid configuration is an effective approach for designing high-accuracy, cost-efficient LEO navigation constellations for future global navigation and precise positioning applications.

title: An adaptive learning-based task offloading framework for IoT applications in volunteer edge–cloud computing
summary: The rapid proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) applications has created increasing demands for low-latency, cost-efficient, and reliable task execution. However, the limited computational capabilities of IoT devices often result in excessive delays, increased energy consumption, and degraded Quality of Service (QoS). Volunteer edge–cloud computing (VECC) has emerged as a promising paradigm that leverages distributed volunteer edge and cloud resources to address these limitations. Nevertheless, efficient task offloading in VECC remains challenging due to resource heterogeneity, dynamic workloads, fluctuating execution costs, heterogeneous QoS requirements, and unpredictable volunteer-node availability. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an adaptive task-offloading framework built upon an enhanced ε-greedy multi-armed bandit (MAB) algorithm. The proposed framework incorporates task-aware learning through separate Q-tables for critical, real-time, and normal tasks, enabling differentiated offloading decisions according to task-specific QoS requirements. Furthermore, a weighted cost model is introduced to jointly optimize monetary execution cost and deadline-violation cost during the learning process, while an adaptive exploration strategy integrating ε scheduling with roulette-wheel–based exploration improves exploration efficiency, learning stability, and convergence in dynamic environments. The proposed framework also incorporates volunteer-resource awareness to effectively accommodate dynamic node participation during online task scheduling. The proposed approach is evaluated through extensive simulation experiments under four representative scenarios involving different traffic loads and volunteer-resource availability conditions. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently achieves lower total cost than the considered baseline approaches, including Random Selection, Round Robin, conventional ε-greedy, and several enhanced ε-greedy variants, while effectively balancing monetary efficiency and deadline compliance. Although the evaluation is simulation-based, the findings indicate that the proposed framework provides an effective lightweight task-offloading solution for dynamic VECC environments and establishes a solid foundation for future trace-driven validation and large-scale experimental evaluation.

title: Intelligent Portfolio Rebalancing with Reinforcement Learning and Dynamic Resource Allocation Under Market Uncertainty
summary: Portfolio rebalancing is a sequential decision problem in which the benefit of moving toward an estimated target must be weighed against trading costs, the risk of breaching a loss limit, and the possibility that the estimate is itself wrong. Calendar rules, threshold rules, and most learning-based portfolio agents treat these considerations in sequence: allocation is optimized first, filtered for turnover second, and examined for risk third. This paper develops a constrained reinforcement learning framework in which friction, risk, and estimation uncertainty enter the decision problem directly. Three components are coupled. The trade vector rather than the target weight is the action, so the self-financing condition and the cost function are structural rather than penalized. An analytically derived no-trade band, obtained from a first-order condition that equates marginal risk reduction to marginal trading cost, is embedded as a feasible-action constraint that the policy cannot violate. A dynamic resource allocation layer maps a scalar uncertainty index and a regime posterior to a risk budget, a trading propensity, and a re-optimization frequency, so that capital and computational attention contract when forecasts are least reliable. The loss limit is imposed as a conditional value-at-risk constraint and handled by Lagrangian dual ascent with ensemble-based tail estimation. The paper derives comparative statics for the band, specifies the conditions under which a learned policy can improve on the analytic rule, and sets out the failure modes and diagnostic protocol that such a system must satisfy before it is allowed to trade. The contribution is a coherent decision architecture whose components are individually interpretable and jointly constrained, rather than a black-box allocation model.

title: DriftShard: Drift-Aware Adaptive Sharding for Distributed Industrial IoT Time-Series Databases
summary: Distributed databases that store Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) telemetry are usually sharded once, by device identifier or by time, and left in that state. The queries that reach them do not stay fixed: operator drill-downs, real-time monitoring and fleet-level analytics alternate over a working day, and each favours a different placement of the data. Re-sharding can recover lost performance, but moving millions of rows is expensive, and a system that re-shards on every change may spend more time migrating than it saves. This paper presents DriftShard, a framework that monitors the mix of query classes reaching a Citus cluster, detects regime changes with a total variation distance test, predicts the latency of every candidate layout with a gradient-boosted cost model, and migrates only when the predicted saving over a planning horizon exceeds the predicted migration time. DriftShard was implemented on PostgreSQL 16 with Citus 12.1 and evaluated with real migrations on a four-node cluster, using a synthetic sensor fleet (0.71 million rows) and the TON IoT telemetry collection (3.58 million rows). Across 40 randomised regime sequences, DriftShard was 42% and 30% faster than a static device-hash layout on the two datasets, and 31% and 53% faster than drifttriggered re-sharding that ignores migration cost. It did not match the best static layout chosen in hindsight, and its benefit depended on cost-model accuracy: with measured rather than predicted costs it improved by a further 6% and 13%. The results identify when adaptive sharding pays off and where learned cost models limit it.

title: An Explainable Machine Learning Framework with Large Language Model Features for Predicting Monetary Redress in Bank Fraud and Scam Complaints
summary: Liability for scam losses is shifting towards banks, yet few interpretable tools can anticipate which fraud and scam complaints will end in redress. This study develops SCAM-XD, an explainable framework that predicts whether a complaint to the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) flagged as possible fraud or a scam closes with monetary relief reported by the company. From the CFPB narratives archive, the study builds a benchmark of these complaints, about half of which human coders confirm as fraud or scams. A large language model (LLM) codes each narrative for scam type, payment rail, authorisation, manipulation cues and signals of the bank's response, agreeing closely with human coding on scam type. These features are combined with structured fields, company identity and text representations in a stacking ensemble, explained with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and linked to a cost-sensitive triage layer. Tested on a later period, SCAM-XD improves significantly on strong baselines across seeds, including a reimplemented topic model approach. LLM features yield a compact, interpretable model that nearly matches a high-dimensional text baseline but do not significantly improve the full model. Company identity is the strongest driver of predicted redress, yet firm identity alone predicts far less well, and payment rail and bank response cues act in directions consistent with liability rules. Under assumed costs, thresholds selected on validation data substantially reduce modelled expected cost relative to standard thresholds, whereas model choice matters much less. Redress depends on both the firm and the facts that determine liability.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Optimizing Component Selection and Assembly Sequences in Customized Manufacturing
summary: Customized manufacturing requires rapid decisions about which variant components to select and in what order they should be assembled, yet the two decisions are usually treated separately. Component selection is governed by requirement compatibility, interface geometry, inventory, and cost, while assembly sequencing is governed by precedence, accessibility, tooling, and stability. This separation produces locally plausible plans that fail when a chosen part creates an infeasible fastening order or when an efficient sequence requires unavailable tooling. The manuscript develops a graph-based formulation in which components, interfaces, operations, resources, and requirement attributes are represented in a heterogeneous product-assembly graph. A constraint-aware graph neural network learns node and edge embeddings through edge-conditioned message passing, predicts component-selection scores, and emits assembly actions through a feasibility-masked sequence decoder. The decoder integrates beam search with constraint filtering and a cost-sensitive objective that balances assembly time, handling effort, quality risk, and reconfiguration. A multi-task training formulation combines supervision, policy learning, cost regularization, and uncertainty estimation, while an entropy-based uncertainty signal identifies states that require conservative fallback to exact search or human review. The contribution is a coherent methodological framework for joint selection-and-sequencing decisions, a set of mathematical relationships that make manufacturing constraints explicit inside learned inference, and a technical discussion of generalization, failure modes, and deployment conditions. The approach is positioned as a decision-support layer for customized production rather than a replacement for engineering validation.

title: Probabilistic remaining useful life prediction using Bayesian Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks
summary: In high-reliability industrial systems, remaining useful life (RUL) prediction of rolling bearings requires not only accurate point estimates but also reliable uncertainty quantification for maintenance decision-making. However, most existing deep learning methods are deterministic, providing only point predictions and failing to separate data noise from epistemic uncertainty. Moreover, their black-box nature makes it difficult to explain how degradation features influence the model predictions used for maintenance decisions. To address these issues, this paper proposes a probabilistic prediction and risk-aware assessment framework based on the Bayesian Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (B-KAN). B-KAN extends the standard Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (KAN) by introducing variational inference and treating the B-spline control points on network edges as random variables, enabling the model to output RUL predictions together with their predictive distributions. Based on the additive structure of KAN, a network-wide path-response approximation is developed to characterize how degradation features influence the model output over time. A maintenance strategy is further designed by optimizing the expected cost rate using the predicted RUL distribution. Experiments on the XJTU-SY and FEMTO-ST datasets demonstrate that B-KAN achieves competitive point prediction accuracy and favorable probabilistic performance in terms of continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), prediction interval coverage probability (PICP), and mean prediction interval width (MPIW). Across the evaluated cost ratios and reliability requirements, the proposed maintenance strategy reduces the ECR by 6.79%–16.66% relative to deterministic KAN, indicating that its economic benefit depends on the specified decision preferences.

title: Application of Computer Vision and Deep Learning for Obstacle Detection in Autonomous Hospital Delivery Robots
summary: Hospital delivery robots must detect obstacles that a single laser scanner handles poorly, including glass doors, thin IV stands, low trolley bases, wheelchairs and stretchers. This article presents a computer-vision and deep-learning obstacle detection system for autonomous hospital delivery robots. A lightweight convolutional detector based on the YOLOv8-nano family is fine-tuned on a hospital-specific dataset of 7,200 images and 31,500 instances in eight classes, extended with a smallobject detection head, an attention module, hospital-specific augmentation and Soft-NMS. Detections are fused with depth from an RGB-D camera to estimate obstacle position, and a class-aware risk policy converts them into semantic costmap inflation and speed limits for an A* and dynamic window navigation stack. The detector reaches 93.1% mAP@ 0.5 and 69.0% mAP@ 0.5: 0.95 at 31 frames per second on an embedded GPU module, with only 3.9 million parameters. It keeps mAP@ 0.5 above 85% in low light, glare, motion blur and partial occlusion. Depth-based ranging has a mean error of 4.8 cm at 2 m. In 200 navigation trials, adding vision raised mission success from 82.0% to 95.5% and eliminated contact collisions (11 with LiDAR alone). The results show that a low-cost vision layer substantially improves the safety of hospital delivery robots.

title: Enhancing Predictive Accuracy with Hybrid Statistical–Deep Learning Models for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting: A Systematic Review with Taxonomy and …
summary:
Introduction: Multivariate time series forecasting has become essential for decision-making in complex domains, including energy, healthcare, finance, and environmental monitoring. Traditional statistical models offer interpretability and efficiency but struggle with nonlinear dependencies, whereas deep learning models capture complex patterns yet often require large datasets and lack transparency. This systematic literature review addresses these limitations by examining the role of hybrid statistical–deep learning models in improving multivariate forecasting performance.
Methodology: Following the PRISMA 2020 framework, studies published between 2020 and 2025 were identified from ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, Springer Nature Link, ACM Digital Library, and Taylor & Francis. From 2,526 identified records, 1,371 records were screened, 376 advanced to detailed eligibility review, 58 full-text reports were assessed, and 44 studies were included in the final synthesis. The selected studies were analysed according to hybrid architecture, forecasting horizon, dataset characteristics, performance outcomes, and methodological limitations.
Results: The review identified four major hybrid categories: residual/error-correction, feature-level, ensemble, and optimisation hybrids. Findings indicated that hybrid models generally outperformed standalone statistical and deep learning approaches, with reported improvements ranging from approximately 5% to over 40% depending on application context, forecasting horizon, and evaluation methodology. Residualbased approaches such as ARIMA–LSTM and VAR–LSTM were effective for combining linear pattern extraction with nonlinear learning, while decomposition and Transformer-based hybrids demonstrated advantages in complex long-term forecasting. However, challenges related to computational cost, interpretability, uncertainty modelling, and deployment feasibility remained.
Conclusion: This review contributes a structured taxonomy, decision-oriented framework, and analysis of failure conditions to support evidence-based selection of hybrid forecasting models.
